title: AI agents, honestly
description: Three different things get called «an agent», and buying the wrong one is expensive. Covers what each actually is, defining a job narrow enough to test, connecting data without granting too much, the four predictable failures, and how the work is priced.

modules.title: The course
modules.description: Five lessons on building and selling assistants that survive contact with real customers.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
«AI agent» is currently used for three different things, and the confusion costs people real money — they buy one and receive another.

Being able to say precisely what you mean is the first commercial skill here, because the scope, the price and the risk are different for each.

blocks.heading: Three things people mean
blocks.bodyHtml:
• A configured chatbot — answers questions from your documents. No actions.
  • An automation — runs a fixed sequence on a trigger. No judgement.
  • An agent — decides which steps to take to reach a goal, and can act.

Most business requests for «an agent» are satisfied by one of the first two, which are cheaper, safer and finishable.

blocks.text: Most people asking for an agent need a configured chatbot or a fixed automation.

blocks.heading: The line that matters
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Build us an AI agent to handle customer enquiries.»

«Answer the eleven delivery questions from our policy document, and hand anything else to a person.»

The second can be tested, corrected and priced. The first cannot even be evaluated — there is no standard to hold it to.

blocks.question: A client wants «an agent» that answers questions from their price list. What is that really?

options.label: A true agent, since it decides how to answer each question.
A configured chatbot — one source, no actions, no decisions.
An automation, because it runs whenever a message arrives.
None of these — answering questions is a separate category.

blocks.successBody: Reading one source and replying is a chatbot. Nothing is decided and nothing happens in the world, which makes it far cheaper to build and far safer to run than what «agent» implies.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask whether anything is decided, and whether anything happens outside the conversation.

blocks.heading: Why the distinction is commercial
blocks.bodyHtml:
A chatbot is a few days and carries almost no risk. An automation is a week and fails visibly. An agent that acts on real systems can do real damage and needs supervision, testing and a rollback plan.

Quoting agent prices for chatbot work loses the job. Quoting chatbot prices for agent work loses money and, eventually, the client.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a request you have heard and sort it into one of the three.
Write what it would need to decide, and what it would change in the world.
If neither, it is a chatbot — say so plainly to the client.
Note how the price you would quote changes with each answer.

blocks.title: Match the request to what it actually needs
blocks.subtitle: Match each thing a business asks for with the right build.

left.text: Answer questions from our returns policy

right.text: A configured chatbot: one source, no actions

left.text: Copy new orders into the sheet every morning

right.text: A fixed automation: same steps, every time

left.text: Work out which supplier to reorder from

right.text: A true agent: it has to decide something

blocks.failHint: Ask two questions of each: is anything decided, and does anything change outside the chat?

blocks.heading: Start at the cheap end
blocks.bodyHtml:
Almost every successful project in this area started as the simplest of the three and grew. Almost every failed one started as the most ambitious.

Build the chatbot, prove it works, then propose the next step with evidence. That sequence is also how you get paid twice instead of once.

blocks.body: «Agent» means three different things: a configured chatbot with one source, a fixed automation, or something that genuinely decides and acts. Most requests are satisfied by the first two, which are cheaper, safer and finishable — and starting there is how the project succeeds.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: scoping the one job an assistant will actually do.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The difference between an assistant used daily and one opened twice is decided before any configuration happens — in how narrowly the job was defined.

General assistants get abandoned because nobody can tell whether they are working.

blocks.heading: Write it like a job advert
blocks.bodyHtml:
«An assistant that helps the team with customer emails.»

«Drafts replies to the eleven delivery questions we get weekly, using our shipping policy, and passes anything else to a person.»

The second names a task, a source and a boundary. Those three make it testable, and testable is what makes it trustworthy.

blocks.text: If you would not hire a person on this description, it is not defined well enough to build.

blocks.heading: Four sections that define the job
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Tasks — countable, nothing vague
  • Sources — exactly which documents it may use
  • Refusals — what it must never answer or promise
  • Escalation — the words it uses to hand over

Writing this document is most of the work. Configuration afterwards is usually an afternoon.

blocks.question: Before configuring anything, what should you ask the client for?

options.label: Access to their systems so you can begin connecting things up.
The last fifty real enquiries, to see what actually gets asked.
A list of features they would like the assistant to eventually have.
Their budget, so the scope can be matched to what they can spend.

blocks.successBody: Fifty real enquiries usually show that a handful of questions cover most of the volume. That is the scope of version one, and it turns a vague project into a small finishable one.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what would tell you which questions actually matter to this business.

blocks.heading: Sell the definition separately
blocks.bodyHtml:
That one-page description is a paid first stage. Two hours of work, genuinely useful even if they stop there, and it protects you from building against a moving target.

It also filters. A client who will not pay for two hours of definition was not going to be a good client for the twenty hours after it.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick a business you know and name one job an assistant could do there.
Ask for or imagine the last fifty enquiries and count the recurring ones.
Write the four sections in one page.
Read it as a job advert — would you hire someone on it?

blocks.title: Match the section to what it prevents
blocks.subtitle: Match each part of the definition with the failure it removes.

right.text: An assistant nobody can judge as working or not

left.text: Words it uses to hand over

right.text: A customer stuck in a loop with no way out

blocks.failHint: Ask what would go wrong if that one section were missing from the page.

blocks.heading: Version one should feel too small
blocks.bodyHtml:
If the first version does not feel almost trivially narrow, it is too big. Narrow ships, gets used, and earns the second version.

Broad gets built, gets tested vaguely, and gets quietly abandoned — usually without anyone telling you why.

blocks.body: Define one job as if writing a job advert: tasks, permitted sources, hard refusals, escalation wording. Scope version one from fifty real enquiries, sell the definition as a paid first stage, and make the first version narrow enough that it feels almost too small.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
An assistant becomes useful when it can reach real information, and dangerous at exactly the same moment. Both come from the same change.

The question is never «what can we connect» but «what is the least it needs to do this job».

blocks.heading: Read before write
blocks.bodyHtml:
Connecting the assistant to the system with full permissions so it can do whatever is needed.

Read-only access to the two documents the job requires, and nothing else.

Reading is recoverable. Writing changes someone's data, and a confident mistake becomes a real problem rather than a wrong answer.

blocks.text: Reading is recoverable. Writing is not. Start with read-only and stay there as long as possible.

blocks.heading: Four rules for access
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Least access — only the sources named in the definition
  • Read-only first — add writing only with a human approving each one
  • Its own credentials — never a person's login
  • A log — what it read, what it did, when

The fourth is what lets you answer «what happened» later. Without it, an incident becomes a guess.

blocks.question: The assistant needs to check order status. What access should it have?

options.label: Full access to the orders system, so nothing blocks it later.
Read-only access to order status, and nothing beyond that.
The same account a support agent uses, for simplicity.
Write access too, so it can update orders when asked.

blocks.successBody: Checking status needs reading, not writing, and nothing else in the system. Shared logins also make every action untraceable, which matters the first time someone asks what happened.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask what the job literally requires, then refuse to grant anything beyond it.

blocks.heading: Give it the right documents, not all of them
blocks.bodyHtml:
Pointing an assistant at an entire shared drive produces confident answers from outdated files. Someone's draft from two years ago is indistinguishable from current policy.

Name the documents. Check their dates. Agree with the client who keeps them current — that person, not you, owns the answers afterwards.

blocks.heading: Try
items: List everything the assistant would need to read for its one job.
Cut anything not strictly required and note why.
Check the date on every source document.
Write down who is responsible for keeping each one current.

blocks.title: Match the access choice to its consequence
blocks.subtitle: Match each decision about permissions with what it produces later.

right.text: A wrong answer at worst, and it is correctable

left.text: Write access to the live system

right.text: A confident mistake that changes real data

left.text: Pointing it at the whole shared drive

blocks.failHint: Ask what the worst realistic outcome of each choice looks like on a bad day.

blocks.heading: Write access needs a human
blocks.bodyHtml:
When the job genuinely requires changing something, put a person between the decision and the action: the assistant proposes, someone approves, then it executes.

Clients accept this readily — it is how they would supervise a new employee — and it removes almost all of the risk while keeping most of the speed.

blocks.body: Connect the least it needs: read-only, named documents, its own credentials, and a log of what it did. Never point it at an entire drive, check the dates on every source, agree who keeps them current, and put a person between any decision and any write.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every assistant that runs long enough will say something wrong. Planning for that is not pessimism — it is the difference between an incident and a crisis.

The failures are predictable, which means most of them can be designed out before launch.

blocks.heading: Four failures you should expect
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Confident invention — an answer that sounds like policy and is not
  • Outdated source — correct answer from a document nobody updated
  • Scope creep in use — people asking it things it was never meant to handle
  • Silent breakage — it stops working and nobody notices

The last is the worst, because there is no complaint to alert you. It just quietly stops.

blocks.text: The dangerous failure is not the wrong answer. It is the wrong answer nobody reports.

blocks.heading: Design the refusals first
blocks.bodyHtml:
Instructing it to be careful and accurate when discussing refunds.

Making refunds a topic it never answers, routed to a person every time.

Asking a model to be careful is a preference. A hard topic ban is a rule, and rules survive the model behaving unpredictably next month.

blocks.question: During testing it invents a delivery time not present in any document. What is the fix?

options.label: Add more documents so the correct information is available to it.
Make delivery a banned topic, routed to a person every time.
Instruct it to be more careful and precise about delivery times.
Accept it as rare, since most customers will not ask about it.

blocks.successBody: Anything the business would be held to — dates, prices, promises — belongs behind a hard route to a human. Instruction quality is not a guarantee, and this is the class of error that reaches customers.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask which fix still holds if the model behaves differently after an update.

blocks.heading: Launch quietly
blocks.bodyHtml:
Do not switch it on for every customer on day one. Run it internally, or have it draft replies a person approves, for two weeks.

Real questions are never the ones you tested for. A soft launch surfaces them while every mistake is still private and cheap.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write the three topics your assistant will always refuse.
Spend twenty minutes trying to make a test version say something wrong.
Write down everything that worked — those are your test cases.
Plan the two-week soft launch and who approves during it.

blocks.title: Match the failure to its safeguard
blocks.subtitle: Match each predictable failure with the thing that prevents it.

left.text: It invents a price that sounds official

right.text: A hard topic ban routed to a person

left.text: It answers from a document nobody updated

right.text: A named owner and a date on every source

left.text: It stops working and nobody notices

right.text: An alert to a named person when it fails

blocks.failHint: For each failure, ask what would have caught it before a customer did.

blocks.heading: Agree the incident procedure before launch
blocks.bodyHtml:
Decide in advance who is told, how quickly it is corrected, and who speaks to the affected customer.

Having that conversation before launch turns an alarming event into a procedure. Having it afterwards, under pressure, is how a good project ends badly.

blocks.body: Expect four failures: confident invention, outdated sources, use beyond scope, and silent breakage. Design hard refusals rather than careful instructions, launch softly with human approval for two weeks, alert a named person on failure, and agree the incident procedure before anyone goes live.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
This is the most valuable thing in this whole catalogue to be able to sell, and the easiest to price wrong — because the build is only part of what the client is buying.

An assistant is not a file you hand over. It keeps running, on live inputs, in a business that changes.

blocks.heading: Three things to charge for
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The definition — the one-page job description, paid separately
  • The build — priced against the work it replaces, not your hours
  • The care — a monthly fee for review, fixes and updates

Most freelancers charge for the middle one only, then do the other two free. That is how a profitable project becomes an unpaid support job.

blocks.text: An assistant is not delivered. It is handed over and then kept alive.

blocks.heading: Price the replacement, not the hours
blocks.bodyHtml:
«It took me eleven hours, so that is eleven hours at my rate.»

«This handles about sixty enquiries a week that a person answers now. £900 to build, £150 a month to keep current.»

The second is judged against what it replaces. The first prices your typing speed and gets cheaper every time you improve.

blocks.question: A client asks why there is a monthly fee when the assistant already works. What is the honest answer?

options.label: It covers hosting costs and the tools the assistant runs on.
Sources go stale, questions change, and tools update — it needs review.
It is standard practice for this kind of software project.
It guarantees you will be available if anything ever breaks.

blocks.successBody: The business changes and the assistant does not notice. Policies shift, new questions appear, tools update — without review it drifts from correct to confidently outdated, which is worse than not existing.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what actually changes in the months after launch, and who would notice.

blocks.heading: Hand over more than access
blocks.bodyHtml:
Give the client a one-page note: what it does, what it refuses, how to update its sources, how to switch it off.

Keeping that vague does not protect your income. A client who cannot see how it works becomes nervous, and nervous clients stop using things — then stop paying for them.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your three-part price: definition, build, monthly care.
Anchor the build on enquiries or hours it replaces per week.
Write the one-page operating note in plain language.
Draft the sentence explaining why care is not optional.

blocks.title: Match the charge to what it buys
blocks.subtitle: Match each part of the price with what the client actually receives.

right.text: A description precise enough to build and test against

left.text: The build fee anchored on replaced work

right.text: A price judged against value rather than your speed
Someone noticing when it drifts out of date

blocks.failHint: For each, ask what the client would lose if that part were not paid for.

blocks.heading: The monthly review is the product
blocks.bodyHtml:
Read a sample of conversations, fix the misses, add new facts — and report what customers are actually asking.

That last part is worth more than the assistant. A monthly summary of real customer questions is business intelligence the client has never had, and it makes the retainer obviously worth keeping.

blocks.body: Charge three times: the definition, the build anchored on the work it replaces, and monthly care. Hand over an operating note rather than just access, and make the monthly review the product — the summary of what customers actually ask is worth more than the assistant itself.
